lecture.title: Esophagus II: Achalasia, Esophageal Neoplasms and Dysmotility Disorders
golden_tip: Apparent achalasia plus short-duration dysphagia, significant weight loss and age over 60 equals malignancy (pseudoachalasia) until endoscopy proves otherwise: always scope and biopsy BEFORE myotomy or dilation.

Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, chronic spinal pain, diaphragmatic paralysis, supraclavicular nodes or more than 20% weight loss = advanced incurable esophageal cancer.
Heartburn in achalasia comes from fermentation of retained food in the dilated esophagus, NOT true gastroesophageal reflux - do not dismiss new dysphagia as ordinary GERD.
Heller 1914 = anterior PLUS posterior myotomies; the MODIFIED Heller used today = single anterior myotomy with Dor - a classic exam distinction, with excellent results in up to 95%.
About two-thirds of esophageal cancer patients are already incurable at diagnosis; MRI adds NOTHING over CT - stage with CT, EUS, PET, laparoscopy and bronchoscopy for upper-third tumors.

concepts.title: Achalasia - Definition, Pathophysiology and Etiology
concepts.summary_ar: الأكالاسيا تعني حرفياً عدم الارتخاء: فقدان التمعج في المري البعيد مع فشل العاصرة السفلية في الارتخاء أثناء البلع، فيتوسع المري ويحتبس الطعام خلف عاصرة مغلقة مكوناً انسداداً وظيفياً عند الوصل المريئي المعدي. السبب الأشيع مجهول، مع أدوار للمناعة الذاتية (HLA-DQw1 وأضداد العصبونات المعوية) والعدوى المزمنة (الهربس النطاقي والحصبة) ومرض شاغاس المدمر لخلايا العقد داخل الجدار.

sections.heading: Definition and Core Pathophysiology
sections.body_text: **Achalasia** literally means 'does not relax'. It is defined by two inseparable abnormalities: **loss of peristalsis in the distal esophagus** and **failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax** during swallowing. The classic pathophysiology diagram (a rectangular box highlights the junction) shows the gastroesophageal junction - where the esophagus meets the stomach - in cross-section: the esophagus above appears dilated and filled with blue-colored material representing retained food/fluid, the LES is a narrowed, tightly constricted muscular ring at its distal end, and the stomach below (with normal rugae, the gastric folds) is entirely normal - but the opening from the esophagus into the stomach is obstructed by the non-relaxing sphincter. The result is a **functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction** with progressive proximal dilation of the esophageal body (**megaesophagus**) - in other words, the sphincter fails to relax while the body fails to propel. Because the barrier is functional rather than a fixed lesion, dysphagia characteristically affects **both solids AND liquids from the outset**. Chronic stasis of retained material explains the downstream pathology: fermentation (experienced as 'heartburn'), inflammation and ulceration, Candida colonization, regurgitation and recurrent aspiration. Whatever the initiating cause, the final common pathway is **loss of the inhibitory ganglion cells of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus** of the distal esophagus and LES, leaving the sphincter unable to relax on swallowing.
key_points: Achalasia means 'does not relax': aperistalsis of the distal esophageal body PLUS failure of LES relaxation
The non-relaxing LES creates a functional GE-junction obstruction with proximal megaesophagus
Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the very beginning - functional, not a fixed mechanical block
Stasis drives fermentation, inflammation, ulceration, candidiasis, regurgitation and aspiration

sections.heading: Etiology
sections.body_text:
The etiology of achalasia **is not known** in the great majority of patients (idiopathic disease). Recognized associations and causes:
- **Autoimmune theory**: achalasia is associated with **HLA-DQw1** and with **antibodies to enteric neurons**, supporting immune-mediated destruction of the esophageal nerve plexuses.
- **Chronic viral infection**: **herpes zoster virus and measles virus** have both been implicated in chronic injury of the esophageal neural plexuses.
- **Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi)**: the classic secondary cause in endemic areas - the organism causes a **loss of intramural ganglion cells**, which leads to **aperistalsis and incomplete LES relaxation**, a picture clinically and manometrically indistinguishable from idiopathic achalasia.
- **Pseudoachalasia** (a mimic rather than a true cause): malignancy infiltrating the esophageal neural plexuses or acting as a paraneoplastic syndrome, other tumors (esophagus, lung, lymphoma, pancreatic carcinoma) and long-term gastric band use - discussed in detail with esophageal cancer.
Whatever the cause, the unifying lesion is **degeneration and loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus** of the distal esophagus and LES.
key_points: Etiology usually unknown (idiopathic)
Autoimmune association: HLA-DQw1 with antibodies to enteric neurons
Chronic infections implicated: herpes zoster and measles viruses
Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) destroys intramural ganglion cells: aperistalsis + incomplete LES relaxation

concepts.title: Achalasia - Clinical Manifestations and Diagnostic Evaluation
concepts.summary_ar: يُشتبه بالأكالاسيا سريرياً بعسر بلع للصلب والسائل مع مناورات التفريغ (الوقوف ورفع الذراعين وشرب الماء بكثرة)، وتؤكد التشخيص ثلاث أدوات: الباريوم بمنقار الطائر ودقة تقارب 95% مع غياب التمعج وربما شكل نشط تشنجي، والمانومتري بضغط عاصرة راجع مرتفع وارتخاء ناقص وغياب التمعج أو تقلصات متزامنة، والمنظار وجوباً لاستبعاد الخباثة، ويظهر مرياً متوسعاً فيه بقايا طعام والتهاب وتقرح ومبيضات، والعاصرة لا تفتح تلقائياً لكنها تُعبر بضغط لطيف.

sections.heading: Clinical Manifestations and Emptying Maneuvers
sections.body_text:
**Dysphagia** is the cardinal symptom of achalasia. Because the esophagus empties poorly, patients adopt characteristic **maneuvers to aid esophageal emptying**:
- **Standing after eating**, to enlist the aid of gravity.
- **Raising the arms after eating**, to increase intrathoracic pressure.
- **Using a large amount of water** to wash the food down.
Other clinical facts from the lecture:
- **Recurrent aspiration** may result from chronic gastroesophageal regurgitation and may lead to **pulmonary complications** (nocturnal cough, recurrent pneumonia).
- **Heartburn is complained of more often than true GER**: it occurs because of **fermentation of retained food in the dilated esophagus**, not because of acid reflux across the tight sphincter.
- The diagnosis is **usually made between the ages of 25 and 60 years**.
- Other symptoms: **chest pain, regurgitation, dyspepsia, weight loss and aspiration**.
- Achalasia carries an **increased risk for developing esophageal cancer of the squamous cell type**, which justifies long-term surveillance even after successful treatment.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids is the cardinal symptom
Emptying maneuvers: standing (gravity), raising arms (raises intrathoracic pressure), large volumes of water
Heartburn = fermentation of retained food, NOT true reflux
Recurrent aspiration from regurgitation causes pulmonary complications
Usually diagnosed between 25 and 60 years of age
Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus

options: Fermentation of retained food in the dilated esophagus

check.explanation_ar: الحرقة في الأكالاسيا ناتجة عن تخمّر الطعام المحتجز في المري المتوسع وليس عن قلس حقيقي عبر عاصرة مشدودة؛ لهذا لا تستجيب الحرقة لمثبطات الحموض كما يُتوقع. المبيضات قد تسبب التهاباً لكنها ليست سبب الحرقة في كل الحالات، والقلس عبر عاصرة مرتخية يناقض أساس المرض.

sections.heading: Barium Swallow (Esophagram)
sections.body_text: The **barium swallow** is the classic radiographic investigation. In achalasia it shows a **significantly dilated esophagus (megaesophagus), reflecting accumulation of ingested material that cannot pass, tapering to a smooth, narrow, beak-like segment at the gastroesophageal junction - the bird's beak (rat's tail) appearance** - classically appreciated on a lateral or oblique projection, where the contrast column ends in a smooth tapered beak above the stomach. **Clinical significance:** the smooth tapering creates a silhouette that resembles the beak of a bird - the classic radiographic sign of achalasia. Fluoroscopy demonstrates **absence of peristalsis** in the esophageal body. The **diagnostic accuracy of the barium swallow is approximately 95%**. In some patients, rather than a flaccid silent tube, **spastic contractions are seen in the esophageal body - the so-called 'vigorous' achalasia** variant. Paired esophagrams of the same patient show the identical picture of smooth distal tapering with proximal dilation; an identical radiographic appearance can, however, be produced by malignant pseudoachalasia, which is why radiology alone never completes the diagnostic workup.
key_points: Bird's beak (rat's tail): smooth tapered GE-junction narrowing with dilated esophagus above
Diagnostic accuracy approximately 95%
Absent peristalsis on fluoroscopy
Spastic body contractions define 'vigorous' achalasia

check.prompt: The diagnostic accuracy of the barium swallow in achalasia is approximately:
options: Only 30%
check.explanation_ar: دقة صورة الباريوم في تشخيص الأكالاسيا تقارب 95% بفضل مظهر منقار الطائر مع غياب التمعج، ومع ذلك يبقى التنظير إلزامياً لاستبعاد الأكالاسيا الكاذبة الورمية قبل أي علاج نهائي.

sections.heading: Esophageal Manometry - the Confirmatory Test
sections.body_text:
**Manometry is the confirmatory diagnostic test** for achalasia and demonstrates the defining triad:
- **Elevated resting LES pressure** (a hypertensive sphincter at rest).
- **Incomplete LES relaxation** with swallowing (failure of deglutitive relaxation).
- **Peristalsis is absent, or replaced by simultaneous (non-propulsive) contractions** in the esophageal body.
Technically, the esophageal motility study measures pressures **at various points in the esophagus after the patient takes wet (fluid-containing) or dry (solid-containing) swallows**. Manometry also separates achalasia from the other dysmotility syndromes - nutcracker esophagus, diffuse esophageal spasm and isolated hypertensive LES - each of which has a distinct pressure signature, and it is essential when the radiographic picture is atypical or when botulinum toxin, pneumatic dilation or surgical myotomy is being planned.
key_points: Elevated resting LES pressure
Incomplete LES relaxation with deglutition
Absent peristalsis or simultaneous contractions in the esophageal body
Performed with wet and dry swallows, measuring pressures at multiple esophageal levels

sections.heading: Endoscopy and Features Suggesting Malignancy
sections.body_text:
**Endoscopy is mandatory in every patient with suspected achalasia** - above all to **exclude malignancies** (pseudoachalasia) before any destructive therapy such as pneumatic dilation or myotomy. Endoscopic findings in achalasia:
- A **dilated esophagus containing residual food material**.
- **Inflammation and ulceration** of the stasis-exposed mucosa.
- **Candida infection** favored by chronic stasis.
- The **LES does not open spontaneously** but is **traversed easily with gentle pressure** - a fixed, impassable, ulcerated or frayed cardia should instead suggest tumor.
**Features that suggest malignancy in a patient with apparent achalasia:**
1. **Short duration of dysphagia.**
2. **Significant weight loss.**
3. **Age older than 60 years.**
Any of these should trigger biopsy and a full oncological workup rather than antispasmodic or mechanical therapy for 'benign' achalasia.
key_points: Endoscopy excludes malignancy (pseudoachalasia) before treatment
Dilated esophagus with residual material, inflammation, ulceration and Candida from stasis
LES does not open spontaneously but is traversed easily with gentle pressure
Malignancy warning triad: short dysphagia duration, significant weight loss, age older than 60

concepts.title: Achalasia - Therapeutic Approaches
concepts.summary_ar: أربع وسائل علاجية للأكالاسيا: الأدوية مرخية العضل الملساء (النترات وحاصرات قنوات الكالسيوم) وآثارها الجانبية الشائعة الصداع والوذمة المحيطية، وسم البوتولينوم الذي يحجب إطلاق الأستيل كولين في الضفيرة العضلية ويناسب غير المؤهلين للجراحة، والتمديد البالوني الذي يضعف العاصرة بتمزق أليافها، والرأب الجراحي بهيلر المعدل: شق أمامي واحد حتى تحت المخاطية مع رأب دور، بنتائج ممتازة حتى 95% عبر طريق صدري أو بطني.

sections.heading: The Four Therapeutic Modalities - Overview
sections.body_text:
There are **four therapeutic modalities** for achalasia:
1. **Pharmacotherapy** (smooth-muscle-relaxing drugs).
2. **Botulinum toxin** injection into the LES.
3. **Pneumatic (balloon) dilation** of the LES.
4. **Surgical myotomy** (the Heller operation).
All four share one goal - **reducing the outflow resistance of the non-relaxing LES** - because the aperistalsis of the esophageal body cannot be restored by any therapy. The choice among them depends on the patient's age, general fitness, comorbidity, preference and local expertise: drugs and botulinum toxin suit frail or high-risk patients, pneumatic dilation offers the most effective non-operative definitive option, and surgical myotomy provides the most durable result in fit patients. Even after successful disruption of the sphincter, esophageal emptying remains gravity- and hydrostatic-assisted rather than truly peristaltic.
key_points: Four modalities: pharmacotherapy, botulinum toxin, pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy
All aim to reduce LES outflow resistance; aperistalsis itself is irreversible
Drugs and botulinum toxin for the unfit; dilation or myotomy for definitive therapy
Emptying after any therapy remains gravity-assisted

sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy and Botulinum Toxin
sections.body_text:
**Pharmacotherapy** uses agents that relax smooth muscle and therefore theoretically decrease LES pressure:
- **Nitrates** and **calcium channel blockers (CCB)**.
- **Side effects such as headaches and peripheral edema are common**, which limits long-term use; medical therapy alone provides only modest and short-lived symptom relief.
**Botulinum toxin (BTX)** injected into the LES **reduces the LES pressure by selectively blocking the release of acetylcholine from the presynaptic cholinergic nerve terminals in the myenteric plexus**. By removing the cholinergic excitatory drive to the sphincter muscle, LES tone falls without any mechanical disruption of the wall. The effect is temporary (months) and injections must be repeated; BTX is therefore most useful in elderly or unfit patients in whom pneumatic dilation or surgery carries an unacceptable risk.
key_points: Nitrates and calcium channel blockers theoretically decrease LES pressure
Headache and peripheral edema are the common limiting side effects
BTX blocks acetylcholine release from presynaptic cholinergic terminals in the myenteric plexus
BTX effect is temporary - reserved mainly for unfit patients

sections.heading: Pneumatic (Balloon) Dilation
sections.body_text: **Balloon dilatation weakens the LES by tearing its muscle fibers.** A large balloon is positioned across the gastroesophageal junction and inflated forcefully under endoscopic or radiologic control, producing a controlled partial tear of the circular muscle of the sphincter while aiming to preserve the mucosa. It is the most effective non-operative definitive treatment, but the very mechanism of muscle tearing carries the risk of **esophageal perforation**, which can progress to mediastinitis and require emergency surgery; repeat dilatation sessions are often needed to maintain symptomatic control. Dilation must only be performed after endoscopy has excluded malignancy (pseudoachalasia) and in a setting where perforation can be immediately recognized and managed.
key_points: Pneumatic dilation weakens the LES by tearing its muscle fibers
Most effective non-operative definitive option
Main risk: esophageal perforation - requires emergency surgical backup
Repeat sessions frequently needed; only after malignancy is excluded

sections.heading: Surgical Myotomy - the Heller Operation
sections.body_text:
**Surgical myotomy weakens the LES by cutting its muscle fibers down to the mucosa**, leaving the mucosa intact.
- The operation was **first described by Ernest Heller in 1914**.
- **Originally it consisted of two myotomies: anterior and posterior.**
- The **modified Heller myotomy** used today is a **single anterior myotomy**, commonly combined with a **Dor (anterior partial) fundoplication** to limit postoperative gastroesophageal reflux.
- **Excellent results have been reported in up to 95% of patients in select series**, making myotomy the most durable option, particularly for fit patients.
- Traditionally accomplished by a **transthoracic or transabdominal approach** (today usually performed laparoscopically).
The myotomy extends across the distal esophageal muscle and onto the gastric cardia so that the high-pressure zone is abolished completely; incomplete extension onto the stomach is a recognized cause of persistent dysphagia after myotomy.
key_points: Myotomy cuts LES muscle fibers down to (but not through) the mucosa
Ernest Heller, 1914: originally anterior AND posterior myotomies
Modified Heller: single anterior myotomy, usually with Dor fundoplication
Excellent results in up to 95% of patients in select series
Transthoracic or transabdominal approach

concepts.title: Esophageal Neoplasms - Benign Tumours and Malignant Histotypes
concepts.summary_ar: الأورام الحميدة للمري نادرة وأغلبها غير ظهاري المنشأ: الورم السدوي المعدي المعوي GIST والشحمي وورم الخلايا الحبيبية، وتبقى غالباً صغيرة وبلا أعراض. الخباثات نوعان: حرشفي يصيب الثلثين العلويين ويسود عالمياً، وعوامل خطره الكحول والتبغ والفقر والجرح القلوي والأكالاسيا وبلامر فينسون ونقص الفواكه والخضار والمشروبات الساخنة والإشعاع المنصفي وفيروس الورم الحليمي والأطعمة الملوثة بالفطور، ويصيب الذكور أربعة أضعاف بعد سن 45؛ وغدي يصيب الثلث السفلي ويسود في الغرب وينشأ غالباً من مري باريت (القلس والتبغ والإشعاع) وبسبعة أضعاف لدى الذكور القوقازيين وبقيا خمس سنوات أقل من 25%.

sections.heading: Benign Tumours of the Oesophagus
sections.body_text:
**Benign tumours of the oesophagus are relatively rare.** True epithelial tumours - **papillomas, adenomas and hyperplastic polyps** - do occur, but the **majority of 'benign' tumours are not epithelial in origin** and arise from other layers of the oesophageal wall:
- **Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)**.
- **Lipoma.**
- **Granular cell tumour.**
**Most benign oesophageal tumours are small and asymptomatic**, discovered incidentally at endoscopy or on imaging, and **even a large benign tumour may cause only mild symptoms** - typically slowly progressive dysphagia or vague retrosternal pressure, rather than the relentless dysphagia, odynophagia and weight loss of carcinoma.
key_points: Benign oesophageal tumours are rare
True epithelial types: papilloma, adenoma, hyperplastic polyp
Majority are non-epithelial: GIST, lipoma, granular cell tumour
Usually small and asymptomatic; even large ones cause only mild symptoms

sections.heading: Malignant Tumours - Types, Distribution and Geography
sections.body_text:
**The vast majority of oesophageal cancers are epithelial** and fall into one of two types:
1. **Adenocarcinoma.**
2. **Squamous cell carcinoma.**
Their distribution within the oesophagus and across the world differs systematically:
- **Squamous cell carcinoma generally affects the upper two-thirds** of the oesophagus.
- **Adenocarcinoma affects the lower one-third.**
- **Worldwide, squamous cell cancer is most common, but adenocarcinoma predominates in the West**, where its incidence has been increasing.
The anatomical split matters clinically: an upper- or mid-oesophageal tumour in a smoker is usually squamous, whereas a distal tumour arising in a Barrett segment is usually adenocarcinoma - a distinction that drives the choice of staging investigations (bronchoscopy for upper-third tumours) and of therapy.
key_points: Two epithelial types: adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma
SCC: upper two-thirds - most common worldwide
Adenocarcinoma: lower one-third - predominates in the West
Tumor location predicts histology and guides staging

sections.heading: Adenocarcinoma - Origin, Risk Factors and Prognosis
sections.body_text:
**Origin and risk factors:**
- **Most oesophageal adenocarcinomas arise from Barrett oesophagus** - the columnar metaplasia created by chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux.
- **Risk factors: gastro-oesophageal reflux/Barrett oesophagus (GERD with metaplastic Barrett), tobacco use and exposure to radiation.** (The source slide also begins a list of factors by which risk is reduced, although the items themselves are truncated in the original handout.)
- **Increased rates of oesophageal adenocarcinoma** have been documented, particularly in Western populations.
- Adenocarcinoma **occurs most frequently in Caucasians** and shows a strong gender bias, being **sevenfold more common in men**.
**Pathogenesis:** molecular studies suggest that the progression of Barrett oesophagus to adenocarcinoma occurs **over an extended period through the stepwise acquisition of genetic and epigenetic changes** - the biological rationale for endoscopic surveillance of Barrett and early interception of dysplasia.
**Clinical features:** pain or difficulty in swallowing, progressive weight loss, hematemesis, chest pain, or vomiting; the tumour is **occasionally discovered during evaluation of GERD or surveillance of Barrett oesophagus**.
**Prognosis:** as a result of the advanced stage at diagnosis, **overall 5-year survival is less than 25%**.
key_points: Most arise from Barrett esophagus
Risk factors: GERD/Barrett, tobacco, radiation exposure
Most frequent in Caucasians; sevenfold more common in men
Stepwise genetic and epigenetic progression over an extended period
Features: painful/difficult swallowing, weight loss, hematemesis, chest pain, vomiting
Advanced stage at diagnosis - 5-year survival under 25%

sections.heading: Squamous Cell Carcinoma - Risk Factors and Clinical Features
sections.body_text:
**Risk factors for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma include:**
- **Alcohol and tobacco use** (polycyclic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines).
- **Poverty.**
- **Caustic oesophageal injury.**
- **Achalasia.**
- **Plummer-Vinson syndrome.**
- **Diets deficient in fruits or vegetables.**
- **Frequent consumption of very hot beverages.**
- **Previous radiation to the mediastinum.**
- **Human papilloma virus infection**, implicated in high-risk areas.
- **Fungus-contaminated foods.**
**Epidemiology:** SCC occurs in **adults older than age 45** and affects **males four times more frequently than females**.
**Clinical features:** the onset is **insidious** and the tumour most commonly presents with **dysphagia, odynophagia (pain on swallowing) or obstruction**; **weight loss** follows. **Hemorrhage and sepsis may accompany tumour ulceration.** Occasionally the **first symptoms are caused by aspiration of food via a tracheoesophageal fistula** - a presentation that must never be mistaken for simple recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
key_points: Alcohol and tobacco (polycyclic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines) lead the risk list
Also: poverty, caustic injury, achalasia, Plummer-Vinson, low fruit/vegetable diet, hot beverages, mediastinal radiation, HPV, fungus-contaminated foods
Adults older than 45; males affected four times more than females
Insidious onset: dysphagia, odynophagia, obstruction, weight loss
Ulceration may cause hemorrhage and sepsis
First symptom may be aspiration via tracheoesophageal fistula

concepts.title: Oesophageal Cancer - Spread, Clinical Features, Pseudoachalasia, Staging Investigations and TNM
concepts.summary_ar: ينتشر سرطان المري بثلاث طرق: مباشرة عبر الجدار، ولمفاوياً، ودموياً؛ والانتشار المباشر يكون جانبياً عبر طبقات الجدار وطولياً داخله عبر القنوات اللمفية تحت المخاطية، فلا يكون التصريف اللمفي قطعياً. مبكراً أعراض عسر هضم غير نوعية، ثم عسر بلع وقلس وقيء وألم بلع ونزول وزن؛ ومتأخراً شلل الحنجري الراجع وهورنر وألم فقري مزمن وشلل الحجاب، ونزول وزن يتجاوز 20% وفقد الشهية يجعلان الشفاء مستبعداً. الأكالاسيا الكاذبة أشيع أسبابها الخباثة. التحقيقات: المنظار أولاً، وتنظير القصبات للثلث العلوي بأكثر من 30%، والتنظير البطني للبذر الصفاقي، والمقطعي للنقائل الدموية، والرنين بلا فائدة إضافية، والتنظير فوق الصوتي للعمق والعقد، والبوزيتروني بالـFDG، مع جدول TNM كاملاً.

sections.heading: Patterns of Tumour Spread
sections.body_text:
**Tumours of the oesophagus can spread in three ways:**
1. **Invasion directly through the oesophageal wall** (direct spread).
2. **Via the lymphatics.**
3. **In the bloodstream.**
**Direct spread occurs both laterally, through the component layers of the oesophageal wall, and longitudinally, within the oesophageal wall.** **Longitudinal spread is mainly via the submucosal lymphatic channels of the oesophagus.** Because of this anatomy, **the pattern of lymphatic drainage of the oesophagus is not segmental, as in other parts of the gastrointestinal tract.** Consequently, tumour cells may travel long distances up and down within the submucosal lymphatics before the lesion declares itself, involved lymph nodes may lie far above or below the visible tumour (including cervical and coeliac fields), and generous longitudinal resection margins are required at oesophagectomy - the tumour seen at endoscopy is only the visible tip of the submucosal iceberg.
key_points: Three routes: direct through the wall, lymphatic, bloodstream
Direct spread is lateral (through wall layers) AND longitudinal (within the wall)
Longitudinal spread runs mainly in the submucosal lymphatic channels
Oesophageal lymphatic drainage is NOT segmental, unlike the rest of the GI tract
Nodes may sit far from the visible tumour - resect generous longitudinal margins

sections.heading: Early and Late Clinical Features
sections.body_text:
**Early disease:** non-specific dyspeptic symptoms, or a vague feeling of **'something that is not quite right' during swallowing**; some cancers are diagnosed **during endoscopic surveillance of patients with Barrett's oesophagus**. As disease progresses: **dysphagia**, sometimes also **regurgitation, vomiting, odynophagia and weight loss**.
**Late disease - signatures of local invasion:**
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy** (hoarseness).
- **Horner's syndrome.**
- **Chronic spinal pain.**
- **Diaphragmatic paralysis.**
**Other factors that make surgical cure unlikely:**
- **Weight loss of more than 20 per cent.**
- **Loss of appetite.**
**Signs of disseminated disease on clinical examination:**
- **Cutaneous tumour metastases.**
- **Enlarged supraclavicular lymph nodes.**
**Hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy is a sign of advanced and incurable disease; palpable lymphadenopathy in the neck is likewise a sign of advanced disease.** These examination findings should redirect the entire plan from curative resection toward staging-confirmed palliation.
key_points: Early: non-specific dyspepsia or 'something not quite right' on swallowing; found on Barrett surveillance
Progressive: dysphagia, regurgitation, vomiting, odynophagia, weight loss
Late: recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, Horner's syndrome, chronic spinal pain, diaphragmatic paralysis
Weight loss over 20% and anorexia make surgical cure unlikely
Cutaneous metastases or supraclavicular nodes = disseminated, incurable disease
Hoarseness or palpable neck nodes = advanced disease

sections.heading: Pseudoachalasia
sections.body_text:
**Pseudoachalasia is a radiographic and manometric mimic of achalasia produced by other pathology:**
- **Malignancy is the most common cause of pseudoachalasia.** The mechanism is either **direct invasion of the oesophageal neural plexuses** by tumour, or a **paraneoplastic syndrome**.
- **Other tumors** that can produce it: **carcinoma of the oesophagus, lung, lymphoma and pancreatic carcinoma**.
- **Long-term use of a gastric band can lead to oesophageal dilatation and pseudoachalasia.**
The clinical lesson: a bird's-beak with warning features (short duration of dysphagia, significant weight loss, age over 60) is cancer until endoscopy and biopsy prove otherwise. Treating pseudoachalasia with pneumatic dilation or Heller myotomy both delays cancer therapy and risks perforating an infiltrated cardia.
key_points: Malignancy is the most common cause of pseudoachalasia
Mechanisms: direct invasion of the oesophageal neural plexuses or a paraneoplastic syndrome
Implicated tumors: oesophagus, lung, lymphoma, pancreatic carcinoma
Long-term gastric band use dilates the oesophagus and mimics achalasia

sections.heading: Endoscopy - the First-Line Investigation
sections.body_text:
**Endoscopy is the first-line investigation for most patients.** It provides an **unrivalled direct view of the oesophageal mucosa and any lesion, allowing its site and size to be documented**, and **cytology and/or histology specimens taken via the endoscope are crucial for accurate diagnosis.**
**The chief limitation of conventional endoscopy is that only the mucosal surface can be studied and biopsied** - submucosal longitudinal spread, deep invasion, nodal disease and distant metastases are invisible to it - **so other investigations are therefore usually required to define the extent (stage) of the disease.**
Once the initial diagnosis of a **malignant oesophageal neoplasm** has been made, **patients should be assessed first in terms of their general health and fitness for potential therapies** (performance status, nutrition, cardiopulmonary reserve) before complex staging.
**Transcutaneous ultrasound** has only a limited role: **it is difficult to visualize mediastinal structures with the relatively low-frequency sound waves** used through the chest wall (it remains useful for the neck, supraclavicular nodes and liver). **Barium esophagram** remains complementary - paired films classically show the megaesophagus tapering to a smooth bird's-beak or rat's-tail at the gastro-oesophageal junction in achalasia, an appearance that pseudoachalasia can reproduce exactly.
key_points: Endoscopy: first-line - direct view, documents site and size, yields crucial cytology/histology
Chief limitation: only the mucosal surface is seen and biopsied
General health and fitness assessed first once malignancy is diagnosed
Transcutaneous ultrasound poorly visualizes mediastinal structures (low-frequency waves)
Barium swallow complementary; bird's-beak may equally be pseudoachalasia

sections.heading: Staging Modalities - Bronchoscopy, Laparoscopy, CT, MRI, EUS and PET
sections.body_text:
- **Bronchoscopy:** many middle- and upper-third oesophageal carcinomas (and therefore usually squamous carcinomas) are sufficiently advanced at the time of diagnosis that the trachea or bronchi are already involved (source Figure 62.46). Bronchoscopy **may reveal impingement or invasion of the main airways in over 30 per cent of new patients with cancers in the upper third** of the oesophagus.
- **Laparoscopy:** a useful technique for the **diagnosis of intra-abdominal and hepatic metastases**; it has the advantage of enabling **tissue samples or peritoneal cytology** to be obtained and is **the only modality reliably able to detect peritoneal tumour seedlings**.
- **Computed tomography (CT) scanning:** the **modality most used to identify haematogenous metastases** - distant organs are easily seen and metastases within them are visualised with high accuracy.
- **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): adds no benefit to the CT scan.**
- **Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS):** can determine **the depth of spread of the malignant tumour through the oesophageal wall**, **the invasion of adjacent organs (T4)** and **metastasis to lymph nodes**; it can also detect **contiguous spread downward into the cardia** and **more distant metastases to the left lobe of the liver**.
- **Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scanning:** PET in the context of cancer staging relies on the **generally high metabolic activity (particularly in the glycolytic pathway) of tumours compared with normal tissues**; the patient is given a small dose of the radiopharmaceutical agent **18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)**, which accumulates in glucose-avid tumour tissue and lights it up on the scan.
key_points: Bronchoscopy: airway impingement/invasion in over 30% of upper-third cancers
Laparoscopy: only modality reliably detecting peritoneal seedlings; allows tissue/cytology
CT: most used for haematogenous metastases with high accuracy
MRI adds no benefit over CT
EUS: depth of wall invasion, T4 organ invasion, lymph nodes, cardia and left liver lobe
PET relies on high glycolytic metabolism; tracer is 18F-FDG

sections.heading: TNM Staging Scheme for Oesophageal Cancer (Table 62.2)
sections.body_text:
**T - primary tumour:**
- **Tis: high-grade dysplasia.**
- **T1: tumour invading lamina propria or submucosa.**
- **T2: tumour invading muscularis propria.**
- **T3: tumour invading beyond muscularis propria.**
- **T4a: tumour invading adjacent structures - pleura, pericardium, diaphragm.**
- **T4b: tumour invading adjacent structures - trachea, bone, aorta.**
**N - regional lymph nodes:**
- **N0: no lymph node metastases.**
- **N1: lymph node metastases in 1-2 nodes.**
- **N2: lymph node metastases in 3-6 nodes.**
- **N3: lymph node metastases in 7 or more nodes.**
**M - distant metastases:**
- **M0: no distant metastases.**
- **M1: all other distant metastases.**
**Stage groupings:**
- **Stage 1A: T1N0M0; Stage 1B: T2N0M0; Stage 2A: T3N0M0; Stage 2B: T1-2N1M0.**
- **Stage 3A: T4aN0M0, T3N1M0, T1-2N2M0; Stage 3B: T3N2M0.**
- **Stage 3C: T4aN1-2M0, T4bN0-3M0, T1-4N3M0.**
- **Stage 4: T1-4N1-3M1.**
Staging integrates the modalities above: **EUS for T and N, CT and PET for M, laparoscopy for peritoneal disease, and bronchoscopy for airway invasion in upper-third tumours.**
key_points: Tis = high-grade dysplasia; T1 lamina propria/submucosa; T2 muscularis propria; T3 beyond muscularis
T4a invades pleura, pericardium, diaphragm; T4b invades trachea, bone, aorta
N1 = 1-2 nodes; N2 = 3-6 nodes; N3 = 7 or more
M1 = any distant metastasis; Stage 4 = any T, N1-3, M1
EUS stages T and N; CT/PET stage M; laparoscopy peritoneum; bronchoscopy airway

concepts.title: Oesophageal Cancer - Treatment: Palliation, Curative Surgery, Oesophagectomy Approaches and Recent Advances
concepts.summary_ar: خوارزمية العلاج: اللياقة للجراحة، ثم النقائل الدموية، ثم الغزو المجاور، ثم الانتشار الصفاقي (أي إجابة بنعم تعني تلطيفاً)، ثم العقد اللمفية (إيجابية = علاج متعدد الوسائط، سالبة = جراحة وحدها). ثلثا المرضى غير قابلين للشفاء عند التشخيص، وهدف التلطيف استعادة البلع المريح بأفضل نوعية حياة. مبادئ الاستئصال: هوامش كافية واستئصال لمفاوي يقلل خطأ التحديد المرحلي، وقد يضاف الإشعاع بعد الجراحة عند نقص الهامش خاصة في الحرشفي. الطرق الجراحية: الصدرية البطنية، وإيفور لويس ذات المرحلتين، وماكون بشق عنقي ثالث، وعبر الحجاب دون فتح الصدر. الحديث: الاستئصال المخاطي بالمنظور والعلاج الضوئي، مع علاج مدثر قد يحسن البقيا وكيميائي إشعاعي وحده قد يشفي حالات مختارة.

sections.heading: Treatment Decision Algorithm and Goals of Palliation
sections.body_text:
**Treatment algorithm for malignant tumours - a clinical decision-making flowchart of sequential questions leading to specific management pathways (source slide):**
1. **Is the patient fit for surgery?** If **no** - **palliation**.
2. If fit: **haematogenous metastases?** If **yes** - **palliation**.
3. **Contiguous organ invasion?** If **yes** - **palliation**.
4. **Peritoneal spread?** If **yes** - **palliation**.
5. **Lymph node metastases?** If **yes** - **multimodal therapy**. If **no** - **surgery alone.**
**Principles:** at the time of diagnosis, **around two-thirds of all patients with oesophageal cancer will already have incurable disease.** The **aim of palliative treatment is to overcome debilitating or distressing symptoms while maintaining the best quality of life possible** for the patient. **Some patients do not require specific therapeutic interventions, but do need supportive care and appropriate liaison with community nursing and hospice care services.**
**Dysphagia is the predominant symptom in advanced oesophageal cancer, so the principal aim of palliation is to restore adequate swallowing.** A variety of methods is available, appropriate to the short life expectancy of most patients (endoscopic stenting, radiotherapy and other endoscopic treatments among them).
key_points: Algorithm: fitness, then haematogenous mets, contiguous invasion, peritoneal spread, then nodes
Unfit / haematogenous mets / contiguous invasion / peritoneal spread = palliation
Node-positive but otherwise clean = multimodal therapy; node-negative = surgery alone
Two-thirds of patients are already incurable at diagnosis
Palliation aims at symptom relief and quality of life; principal target is swallowing
Some patients need only supportive, community and hospice care

sections.heading: Curative Surgery - Principles of Oesophagectomy
sections.body_text:
**The principle of oesophagectomy is to deal adequately with the local tumour in order to minimize the risk of local recurrence, and to achieve an adequate lymphadenectomy to reduce the risk of staging error.**
- **When such a margin cannot be achieved proximally - particularly with squamous cell carcinoma - there is evidence that postoperative radiotherapy can minimize local recurrence.**
- **Adenocarcinoma commonly involves the gastric cardia** and may therefore **extend into the fundus or down the lesser curve**; **some degree of gastric excision is essential** in order to achieve adequate local clearance and accomplish an appropriate lymphadenectomy.
- **Excision of contiguous structures - such as the crura, diaphragm and mediastinal pleura - needs to be considered** as a method of creating **negative resection margins.**
A radical resection therefore removes the tumour-bearing oesophagus with generous longitudinal margins (respecting submucosal spread), a sleeve of stomach when required for cardia/fundus disease, the appropriate lymph-node fields, and any contiguous structure invaded en route - en bloc, with immediate reconstruction, usually by a gastric conduit.
key_points: Adequate local tumour clearance minimizes local recurrence
Adequate lymphadenectomy reduces the risk of staging error
Inadequate proximal margin (especially SCC): postoperative radiotherapy reduces recurrence
Cardia involvement demands partial gastric excision along the fundus and lesser curve
Crura, diaphragm and mediastinal pleura may be excised to obtain negative margins

sections.heading: Surgical Approaches to Oesophagectomy (Figure 62.53)
sections.body_text:
**The two usual approaches for surgery of the oesophagus (Figure 62.53):**
- **(a) Thoracoabdominal approach:** a single long, curved incision extending from the **left lower chest across the costal margin into the upper abdomen**, which **opens the abdominal and thoracic cavities together**; the stomach is mobilized, **pulled up and tubularized to replace the resected oesophagus.**
- **(b) Two-stage Ivor Lewis approach:** **the abdomen is opened first, closed, and then the thoracotomy is performed** - a right thoracotomy plus a vertical upper midline laparotomy in the mid-abdomen; the **gastric conduit is positioned within the thoracic cavity for the anastomosis.**
- **The McKeown operation adds a third incision in the neck to complete a cervical anastomosis.**
- **(3) Transhiatal oesophagectomy: performed without thoracotomy** - the oesophagus is mobilized through the abdominal hiatus and a cervical incision, and the anastomosis is cervical.
Choice of approach depends on tumour location (upper-third tumours favour a cervical anastomosis; distal adenocarcinomas suit Ivor Lewis or thoracoabdominal), the need for mediastinal lymphadenectomy, and the patient's cardiopulmonary reserve.
key_points: Thoracoabdominal: one incision, chest and abdomen opened together; stomach tubularized as conduit
Ivor Lewis: abdomen first, then right thoracotomy; intrathoracic anastomosis
McKeown: third cervical incision completes a cervical anastomosis
Transhiatal oesophagectomy avoids thoracotomy altogether
Approach follows tumour location, nodal fields and cardiopulmonary fitness

sections.heading: Recent Advances (EMR, PDT) and the Summary Points
sections.body_text:
**Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR):** for apparently **early lesions**, EMR has become **increasingly popular**, providing **either a cure or at least sufficient histological information upon which to base a further management strategy** (precise T-staging of high-grade dysplasia and early cancer).
**Photodynamic therapy (PDT):** an alternative approach **largely used in patients who were either unfit or unwilling to undergo surgery**. This endoscopic technique relies on **the administration of a photosensitiser that is taken up preferentially by dysplastic and neoplastic tissue**, which is then destroyed by activating light delivered through the endoscope (systemic photosensitizers add the drawback of cutaneous photosensitivity).
**Summary points of the lecture:**
- **Radical oesophagectomy is the most important aspect of curative treatment.**
- **Neoadjuvant treatments before surgery may improve survival in a proportion of patients.**
- **Chemoradiotherapy alone may cure selected patients, particularly those with squamous cell cancers.**
- **Useful palliation may be achieved by chemo/radiotherapy or endoscopic treatments.**
key_points: EMR for early lesions: cure or definitive histology for further planning
PDT: photosensitiser taken up by dysplastic/neoplastic tissue, activated endoscopically; for unfit/unwilling patients
Radical oesophagectomy remains the cornerstone of cure
Neoadjuvant therapy may improve survival in a proportion
Chemoradiotherapy alone can cure selected SCC patients
Palliation by chemo/radiotherapy or endoscopic treatments

Photodynamic therapy as first-line for all stages

key_terms.definition_ar: استئصال المري الجذري مع إعادة الوصل بأنبوب المعدة؛ حجر الأساس في العلاج الشافي.
استئصال حقول العقد اللمفية مع الورم لتقليل خطر خطأ التحديد المرحلي.
عملية إيفور لويس ذات المرحلتين: فتح البطن أولاً ثم الصدر الأيمن لاستئصال الورم وعمل الوصل داخل الصدر.
